needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Ram: Lakshman can slay all the world's demons in a moment, so there is nothing to fear; and if he has come frightened for refuge, I will guard him like my own life.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Vibhishan, who counts himself low and without one good deed, is gladly held to the Lord's heart.

depicts.why: he calls his own nature low
he says he has never done anything good

heals.why: the welcome comes without his having earned it

cultivates.why: he is astonished at being received

commentary.reading: Vibhishan: I am a nishachara of very low nature who never did a good act, yet the Lord whose form does not come even into sages' meditation gladly embraced me.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram grieves in Sita's grief, and his love for her is twice her own, so she need not feel diminished.

heals.why: the one she misses is suffering her suffering
she is told not to count herself less
the fear of being forgotten is answered by a witness

commentary.reading: Hanuman to Sita in Ashok Vatika: the Lord and his brother are well, but he is sad in your sorrow; do not feel small at heart, mother, Ram's love is twice yours.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Bharat, speechless at the reunion, says he was drowning in separation and Ram took him by the hand.

depicts.why: fourteen years named as a sea he was going under in

cultivates.why: a joy beyond word and thought
he credits the one who reached for him

commentary.reading: Asked his welfare, Bharat cannot speak; then: now I am well, lord of Kosala, you gave darshan knowing your servant distressed and caught my hand as I sank in the ocean of viraha.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The mothers run to Ram like cows running home at dusk to the calves they had to leave, and their pain of separation ends.

depicts.why: the whole day's absence is in the running

cultivates.why: the hard pain of separation is gone and joy is countless

commentary.reading: On Ram's return the mothers rush like cows that left young calves at home and run lowing at day's end; he meets each with love, and the calamity born of separation departs.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram tells Bharat he is spotless in deed, word and mind, and that none is his equal.

heals.why: the one he fears he wronged declares him clean
he is told there is no one like him

needs: that the reader's guilt is larger than anything they actually did

commentary.reading: Ram to Bharat before the elders: in karma, vachan and manas you are pure, your like is only you; how can a younger brother's virtues be told in the guru's assembly at such a time.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Even the wise sage Vasishtha is overcome by sorrow and affection as he speaks of Ram, Lakshman and Sita.

depicts.why: the family's teacher cannot keep his voice steady
he speaks of those who have gone to the forest

heals.why: if the jnani weeps, grief is no lapse of wisdom

commentary.reading: Vasishtha, counselling the court after the king's rites, is himself drowned in shoka and sneha while praising Ram's nature and the love of Lakshman and Sita.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: A mother asks the gods and ancestors to guard her departing son as eyelids guard the eyes.

depicts.why: she cannot go with him, so she hands him to the gods
those left behind are fish and the years of exile their water

cultivates.why: love turned into blessing when it cannot protect

commentary.reading: Kausalya's blessing to Ram: may devas and pitris keep you as the lids keep the eye; the term of exile is water and your dear ones the fish, so return in time.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram tells Hanuman not to feel small: the servant with no other refuge is twice as dear to him as his own brother.

heals.why: he is told not to count himself less
his failure to recognise Ram is answered with affection

cultivates.why: having no other refuge is what makes him dear

commentary.reading: Hanuman, ashamed at not recognising his Lord, falls at Ram's feet; Ram lifts him: do not feel diminished, you are twice as dear as Lakshman; the ananya servant is dear to me.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: A friend tells the grieving Ram to steady his heart and promises to serve in every way until Sita is found.

heals.why: grief is met by someone offering to carry the work
the search now has an ally

cultivates.why: comfort given as a concrete promise of help
he commits himself in every way

commentary.reading: Ram weeps on seeing Sita's cloth; Sugriva says leave sorrow, bring dhira to your mind, I will serve in every way so that Janaki comes back to you.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram takes in whoever comes before him for refuge after a single bow, and never keeps their faults in his heart.

heals.why: faults are seen and not held
one bow is enough to be made his own

cultivates.why: coming before him once

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Bharat on Ram's nature: even the worst, coming before you for sharan, you made your own at a single pranam; you never took their faults to heart and praised their virtues among the good.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram did the poet good out of his own goodness, as water does not drown the grass it has itself nourished.

depicts.why: he calls himself one who wronged his master

heals.why: the care rests on the master's goodness, not his record
low as floating grass, and still not sunk

cultivates.why: trusting the one who raised him

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Ram did me good by his own goodness; I am a traitor to my master, yet he is good to his servant. Water does not sink the straw riding on its head, knowing it watered it.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet is fallen and Hari is the purifier of the fallen, so the two are well matched.

depicts.why: he calls himself fallen without softening it

heals.why: the fall becomes his claim on grace
his worst fact is turned into a fit

cultivates.why: he rests his case on the Lord's name as patit pavan

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas with a devotee's boldness: I have heard Hari is patit pavan; I am patit and you patit pavan, so both our parts are made.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: With nowhere to go and no one who will listen, the poet finds in Ram the only support of the supportless.

depicts.why: no one to tell and no one who would listen
he calls himself one who has lost every limb of support

cultivates.why: Ram's virtues are the prop of those with none

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: where shall I go, whom tell, who hears the lowly; in the three worlds you alone are the refuge of the helpless; lords are many in the world, but your virtues are the support of the supportless.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Repeating Ram's name removes the burning of the heart.

heals.why: the heart's burning is given something to do
a single repeated act to return to

cultivates.why: the burn eases with the name
japa of the name

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Vinay Patrika refrain: by japa of Ram nam the jarani of the heart departs.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'slowly' is added.

claim: There is no other friend of the lowly who feels another's pain, so there is no one else to tell.

depicts.why: no one else would feel his pain if told
he speaks as one of the lowly

cultivates.why: he takes his sorrow to the one who will feel it

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: where shall I find another deenbandhu; who but you feels another's pain; to whom shall I tell my wretchedness.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Afraid of the cruelty of the age, the poet asks Ram to say: Tulsi, you are mine, do not lose heart.

depicts.why: he trusts and is still afraid, looking at the times

heals.why: the words he needs to hear are spoken out
'you are mine'

cultivates.why: he asks only to be claimed

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: hearing your ways my trust and love are in you, yet I fear seeing Kali's havoc; it will be well only if you say or have it said, Ram: Tulsi, you are mine, do not lose heart or tremble.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The line gives only the reply and reads as Ram's direct promise. The verse is a request to hear it. Closer: 'I am afraid. Say it to me, Ram: you are mine, do not lose heart.'

claim: What the poet could not set right in countless ages, Ram sets right in a quarter of a moment.

depicts.why: effort without end that has not mended him

heals.why: the mending is not all his to do
failure at self-repair is no longer final

cultivates.why: handing the making over

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: what I make does not come right in a crore of kalpas; made by you, Ram, it is done in a quarter of an instant.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet asks Ram to look his way and pass over his countless faults, since good or bad he is Ram's own.

depicts.why: he counts his faults as beyond number
he is waiting to be looked at

cultivates.why: 'good or bad, I am yours'

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Raghuvir, will you ever in grace look at me too; knowing your servant, good or bad, as your own, treasury of mercy, will you let my endless faults pass.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: There is no place for the suffering and destitute except the master who shelters even one with no strength left.

depicts.why: every limb without strength
no place anywhere for the hurting and poor

cultivates.why: the only master who keeps the powerless

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: where shall I go, where is a place for the dukhit and deen; who is a master so gracious that he keeps the refugee bereft of strength in every limb.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Telling the gracious Ram all one's merits and faults makes misery lean and contentment full.

heals.why: wretchedness thins when it is spoken
faults are said aloud to someone kind

cultivates.why: contentment grows stout
telling him everything

needs: that the reader is willing to pray

commentary.reading: Dohavali: Tulsi, tell gracious Ram your gunas and doshas; deenata will grow lean and santosha very plump.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

claim: When everyone hinders and no one helps, whatever good comes will come from the gracious Ram.

depicts.why: no one turned out to be a helper
everyone has become everyone's obstacle

cultivates.why: good is expected from Ram alone

commentary.reading: Dohavali: all have become hindrances to all, none a helper; Tulsi, whatever good is to be will be from kripalu Ram.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: 'Somewhere kinder' removes Ram, who is the whole of the second line. Corrected: 'Everyone got in everyone's way and no one helped. Whatever good comes will come from the kind Ram.'

claim: Remembering the feet that freed Ahalya from her curse, give up worry: trouble will end and the heart's hope be met.

heals.why: worry is set down before a known act of release
one cursed and turned to stone was freed

cultivates.why: trust built on what those feet have done

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Dohavali: Tulsidas, remember the feet that released the stone from its curse; leave soch, sankat will vanish and the mind's hope be fulfilled.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: The line drops the ground of the hope, Ram's feet, and reads as a bare assurance that trouble passes. Closer: 'Remember the feet that freed Ahalya. Let the worry go.'

claim: Abandoned by his parents and scorned, Tulsidas once told Ram his hunger and found a master who held nothing against him.

depicts.why: left by mother and father at birth
lowly, dishonoured, hungry for a dog's scraps

heals.why: the master he found laid no fault on him

cultivates.why: he showed his empty stomach just once

commentary.reading: Kavitavali, Uttarakand: mother and father bore and abandoned me, fate wrote no good on my brow; low, scorned, cowardly, craving a dog's morsels. Hearing Ram's nature, Tulsi once showed his belly, and Raghunath proved master for both worlds.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: 'Was held' is looser than the verse, which says Ram proved a master for this world and the next and found no fault. Acceptable in story voice.

claim: Where no friend, spouse, child or parent can go with one, Ram alone forgives every fault and keeps one through the worst.

depicts.why: the place where no one can come along
every crisis at once and a worry with no solution

heals.why: one keeper remains where all others fall away
every fault of body, word and mind forgiven

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: where there is no kind master, no companion, wife, son, brother, father or mother, who but the gracious one quells the dreadful pain; where all is sankat, there my lord Ram keeps me. Read of the hour of death.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: In pain, the poet calls Hanuman water to his fish and mother to his infant, his only support, and asks to be soothed.

depicts.why: a body in pain that cannot wait
he is the infant, wholly dependent

cultivates.why: 'you are my only support'

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: you are water and I the water creature, you mother and I the child; do not delay, my support is you alone; knowing the child distressed, protect him and pass your long tail over Tulsi's arm.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

claim: The suffering poet asks Hanuman to lay a hand on his head: the servant of such a protector should not suffer.

depicts.why: illness that has gone on
he wants a hand on his head

cultivates.why: he asks his protector for one gentle act

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: lord of monkeys, pass your hand over Tulsi's head; with a guardian like you, do not look on while your servant suffers.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

line_issue: 'Let me not be left alone in this pain' interprets. The verse says: do not see your servant suffering.

claim: All troubles and worries tear like spider webs when Hanuman's name is taken.

heals.why: worries are pictured as cobwebs
the name is something to say in the moment

cultivates.why: confidence in calling on Hanuman

needs: devotion to Hanuman

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: Tulsi says all sankat and soch burst like a spider's web on taking your name.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

line_issue: 'The one you trust' removes Hanuman's name. Corrected: 'Troubles and worries tear like cobwebs when your name is taken, Hanuman.'

claim: After Ram leaves, Kausalya holds his childhood bow and little shoes to her heart and sometimes goes to wake him as before.

depicts.why: she presses his small shoes to her heart and eyes
she still goes to wake a child who is not there

commentary.reading: Gitavali, Ayodhya: the mother gazes at his toy bow and arrows, lays his little sandals again and again on heart and eyes, and at times goes as before to wake him: rise, child, your brothers and friends are at the door.
commentary.source: Gita Press Gitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Keeping Ram's name on the tongue lights both the inner and the outer life.

heals.why: a lamp for inside and outside at once

cultivates.why: the name kept at the threshold of the tongue
light within and without

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: place the gem-lamp of Ram nam on the doorsill of the tongue if you want light inside and out. The tongue is the threshold between inner and outer.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Remembering the name even without seeing the form brings a special love into the heart.

heals.why: the unseen Lord is reached through his name

cultivates.why: remembrance of the name
love that rises with the name

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Tulsidas on name and form: a form is not known without its name though it lie in the palm; the name remembered without the form brings the form into the heart with special love.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: In this age neither ritual, devotion nor discernment is within reach; the name of Ram is the one support.

heals.why: when every practice feels beyond one, a support is still left
there is one thing one can still do

cultivates.why: leaning on the name alone

needs: that the reader wants a devotional support

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: in Kali there is no karma, bhakti or viveka to rely on; Ram nam is the only support, the wise and able Hanuman against Kalanemi, the store of deceit.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: In a terrible age the name of Ram is a wish-giving tree, and a father and mother in this world and the next.

heals.why: a guardian is named for a frightening time
the name is called father and mother

cultivates.why: taking the name as one's shelter

needs: that the reader wants a devotional support

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: the name is a kalpataru in the dreadful age, its remembrance quiets the world's snare; Ram nam grants the desired in Kali and is well-wisher, father and mother here and hereafter.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Repeated with love or without, even in irritation or laziness, the name brings good from every direction.

heals.why: the practice works even when done lazily
no right mood is required to begin

cultivates.why: saying the name as one is

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: with good feeling or bad, in annoyance or even sloth, japa of the name brings mangal in all ten directions.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram is a good master who looks from his own side and cares for even a poor servant.

depicts.why: he calls himself a bad servant

heals.why: the care does not depend on the servant's quality

cultivates.why: trusting the master's nature over one's own record

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: he whose kindness is never sated with being kind will mend me in every way; Ram is the good master and I the bad servant, yet he looks to his own nature and nourishes me.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The Lord does not keep a devotee's lapse in mind and remembers the devotee's heart a hundred times.

heals.why: the mistake is not what is remembered
the heart is counted, not the slip

cultivates.why: trust that one is seen by one's intention

needs: that the reader relates to Ram as Lord

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: the Lord's mind does not hold the wrong done and recalls the heart's feeling a hundred times; the very offence for which Bali was slain Sugriva repeated, and Ram overlooked it.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram is pleased by what his servant means in the heart, even when it is badly said.

heals.why: clumsy words do not spoil a true intention
the fear of saying it wrong is lifted

cultivates.why: being understood by the heart

needs: that the reader relates to Ram as Lord

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: what is spoiled in the telling is good in the heart, and Ram is pleased, knowing his servant's mind.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram, who made stones float and monkeys into wise ministers, will honour even a foolish servant's love.

heals.why: unfit material is what he has always worked with

cultivates.why: the one who made stones into boats can use me
he dares to begin his work

needs: that the reader relates to Ram as Lord

commentary.reading: Tulsidas on why he dares to write: gracious Ram will keep the love and liking of a dull servant, he who made rocks into ships and monkeys and bears into counsellors.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The formless, unborn Absolute lies in Kausalya's lap, brought there by love and devotion.

cultivates.why: the infinite held as a child
love is what brings the Lord near

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: the all-pervading, stainless, attributeless, unborn Brahman, beyond play, rests in Kausalya's lap under the sway of prema bhakti. Nirguna made saguna by love.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Knowing the whole world of beings to be filled with Sita and Ram, Tulsidas bows to all with folded hands.

heals.why: every creature is bowed to before the work starts
the poet begins by bowing to all

cultivates.why: reverence toward every being

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: the four classes and 84 lakh kinds of beings in water, land and sky, knowing all the world as Siya Ram maya, I salute with joined palms.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram lives always in the heart of one who wants nothing from him and simply loves him.

heals.why: love with no request attached

cultivates.why: loving without asking
wanting nothing from God

commentary.reading: Valmiki ends his list of Ram's dwelling places: he who never wants anything and has natural love for you, dwell forever in his mind; that is your own house.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Bharat asks for neither wealth, duty, pleasure nor liberation, only love for Ram's feet in every birth.

heals.why: all four aims of life are set aside for one

cultivates.why: love for Ram asked as the only boon
even liberation is not wanted

commentary.reading: Bharat at Prayag to Triveni: I have no relish for artha, dharma or kama, nor do I want nirvana; birth after birth, love for Ram's feet is the boon, no other.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Bharat is good in every way and dearest of all to Ram, so his guilt is baseless.

heals.why: a voice outside him says the guilt is for nothing
no one is dearer to the one he fears he hurt

needs: that the reader's guilt is larger than anything they actually did

commentary.reading: Triveni answers Bharat: child, you are sadhu in every way with fathomless love for Ram's feet; in vain you feel glani, none is as dear to Ram as you.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Whether Ram rejects him or honours him, Bharat's only refuge is Ram's feet; the fault is the servant's.

depicts.why: he walks toward someone who may turn him away
he counts his mind soiled and the fault his own

cultivates.why: refuge that does not depend on the answer

needs: knowing Bharat is blameless; and that the refuge is in God, not in a person who mistreats you

commentary.reading: Bharat on the road to Chitrakoot: whether he abandons me as foul-minded or honours me as servant, my shelter is Ram's sandals; Ram is the good master, all fault is the servant's.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Shame over his mother's deed holds Bharat back, and remembering Ram's nature quickens his steps.

depicts.why: his feet are pulled back by a wrong that was not his
he is unsure of his welcome

heals.why: thinking of the other's nature, not his own record, moves him forward

cultivates.why: devotion carries him like a patient ox

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: his mother's misdeed seems to turn him back, the strength of bhakti bears him on; when he thinks of Raghunath's nature his feet fall quickly on the path.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram understood every distressed person and met each in the way that person longed for.

heals.why: each hurting person is seen separately

cultivates.why: meeting people as they need, not all alike

commentary.reading: At Chitrakoot the compassionate, all-knowing Lord knew all the people to be distressed, and kept regard for each according to the feeling with which each longed.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram is father, mother, friend, teacher and master, who values merits, removes faults and protects those who seek refuge.

heals.why: every close relation is found in one

cultivates.why: he places himself wholly under such a master
he lists what he has in Ram

needs: that the reader relates to Ram as Lord

commentary.reading: Bharat before the assembly: Lord, you are father, mother, friend, guru and master, protector of the surrendered, taker of virtues and remover of faults; no master is like mine.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Though Bharat came against his father's order out of grief and love, Ram looked from his own side and took it all as good.

depicts.why: he admits he came against the order

heals.why: an act done from grief and love is received kindly

cultivates.why: he thanks Ram for reading him generously

commentary.reading: Bharat: from grief, affection or childishness I came setting the command aside; even so, gracious one, looking to your own nature you counted it good in every way.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Though Jayant's offence deserved death, Ram, out of tenderness, let him go when he came for refuge.

heals.why: one who did real harm is still not destroyed

cultivates.why: he is spared only on falling at Ram's feet
mercy given where punishment was just

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram and owns the harm done

commentary.reading: Jayant, as a crow, wounds Sita and is chased by Ram's arrow through the worlds; taking refuge, he is spared his life but, in the Manas, loses one eye. Mercy with a consequence.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: 'Let him go' clips the arc: Ram spares his life but takes one eye. Closer: 'He had done wrong and deserved worse. When he came for shelter, the Lord spared his life out of tenderness.'

claim: Sutikshna finds in himself no devotion, wisdom or practice, and relies on this: the Lord loves one who has no other refuge.

depicts.why: he lists everything he lacks
he is unsure he will be received as Ram's own

heals.why: having nowhere else to go is itself the qualification

cultivates.why: he runs to meet Ram anyway

commentary.reading: Sutikshna, Agastya's disciple, doubts his fitness: no firm trust, no bhakti, virati or jnana, no satsang or japa; yet the compassionate one's habit is that he who has no other gati is dear.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Seeing his devotee's overflowing love, Ram watches from hiding and then appears in his heart.

cultivates.why: love so full that he forgets the road
the Lord comes to one lost in love

commentary.reading: Sutikshna, having gained unbroken prema bhakti, dances on the path; the Lord watches hidden behind a tree and, seeing his great love, manifests in his heart.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram lives always in the power of one who sings his praise with tears and has no lust, pride or pretence.

cultivates.why: devotion felt in the body, voice and eyes
tears of love while singing

commentary.reading: Ram to Lakshman, ending the teaching on bhakti: he whose body thrills singing my virtues, voice choked and eyes streaming, free of kama, mada and dambha, I am ever in his power.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram rests always in the heart of those who make him their goal in word, deed and mind and worship without desire.

heals.why: worship with nothing asked in return

cultivates.why: Ram as the one goal of word, act and thought
the heart as his resting place

commentary.reading: Ram to Lakshman: those whose refuge I am in vachan, karma and mana, who worship nishkama, in the lotus of their heart I always rest.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram touches the dying Jatayu's head, and gazing at Ram's face all Jatayu's pain leaves him.

heals.why: dying is shown held and unafraid
the one who gave everything is not left alone at the end

cultivates.why: the hand laid on the head of the dying

commentary.reading: Raghuvir, ocean of grace, strokes Jatayu's head with his lotus hand; looking at Ram's lovely face the vulture's whole pain departs.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram tells Shabari she is most dear to him and that the state hard for yogis is easy for her today.

heals.why: a forest woman of no rank is told she has what yogis seek

cultivates.why: devotion firm in every form
her worth is declared by Ram himself

commentary.reading: Ram to Shabari: whoever has even one of the nine, woman or man, is most dear to me, and in you all are firm; the gati rare for hosts of yogis is easy for you today.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Shiva says from his own experience that worship of Hari is real and the whole world is a dream.

heals.why: what one clings to is called a dream

cultivates.why: the world held as passing
devotion named as the one real thing

needs: a reader asking what lasts; not someone in fresh loss

commentary.reading: Shiva to Uma: I tell my own anubhava, Hari bhajan is true and all the world a dream.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: 'Love for God' is acceptable for Hari bhajan, but 'the rest passes like a dream' softens 'the whole world is a dream'. Closer: 'I tell you from my own experience: worship of God is real, and the whole world is a dream.'

claim: Ram withholds nothing from his own, and asks that this trust never be given up.

heals.why: hesitation to ask is answered by his nature
nothing is too much to ask

cultivates.why: a trust he asks his devotee never to drop

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Ram to the hesitant Narada: you know my nature, do I ever hide anything from my servant; there is nothing I would not give my own. Narada then asks for love of the Name. Read with the next verses, where Ram explains a refusal.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram guards those who worship him with no other reliance as a mother pulls her child back from fire or a snake.

heals.why: a wish that was blocked is read as a mother's hand
someone is watching where the child runs

cultivates.why: protection includes being stopped

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram; the refusal in question was of his own desire

commentary.reading: Narada asks why Ram prevented his marriage; Ram: those who worship me giving up all other trust I guard always, as a mother holds back the child running at fire or snake.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Gate: the passage that follows this in the Manas speaks of woman as the danger the devotee is guarded from. That part demeans women and must stay out; this verse can stand without it.

claim: The humble devotee is like the Lord's small child and relies on his strength, while the wise rely on their own.

heals.why: being small and dependent is the safer place
relying on one's own strength is the grown son's risk

cultivates.why: leaning on the Lord's strength

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Ram: the jnani is like my grown son and the prideless servant like my infant; my servant has my strength, the jnani his own, and both face kama and krodha. So the wise keep bhakti even after jnana.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Hanuman owns many faults and asks only that the master not forget his servant; the soul is freed by the Lord's tenderness.

depicts.why: he begins by owning many faults
the fear of slipping from the Lord's memory

cultivates.why: release asked from grace, not earned

commentary.reading: Hanuman on recognising Ram: though I have many faults, Lord, let the servant not fall from the master's mind; the jiva is deluded by your maya and crosses only by your kindness.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: One who knows no method of worship can rely on the Lord as a child relies on its mother, and live without worry.

heals.why: the one relied on has to do the looking after
not knowing how to worship is no bar

cultivates.why: a child's reliance
living asoch, free of worry

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Hanuman: I know no means of bhajan; the servant on the master and the son on the mother rely and stay free of care, and the Lord must nourish them.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram lifts the distressed Hanuman, holds him to his heart and cools him with his own tears.

heals.why: the one who fell at his feet in distress is raised and held
the Lord himself weeps at the meeting

cultivates.why: he falls at the feet and is embraced

commentary.reading: Hanuman falls at Ram's feet, showing his own form; Raghupati raises him, clasps him to his heart and soothes him with the water of his own eyes.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Even sinners cross the world's ocean by Ram's name; as his messengers, give up timidity, hold Ram in the heart and act.

heals.why: timidity before the sea is called out by one who has seen worse
a party that gave up is told to find a way

cultivates.why: get up and devise the means
act with Ram held in the heart

commentary.reading: Sampati to the vanaras: sinners who remember his name cross the shoreless bhavasagar; you are his envoys, leave cowardice, keep Ram in your heart and make the effort.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The devotee has no other longing and asks Ram for full devotion and a mind free of desire and its kin.

heals.why: he asks to be rid of desire and the faults that follow it
every other longing is disowned

cultivates.why: a daily prayer for devotion alone

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Tulsidas's mangalacharan to Sundar Kand: Raghupati, there is no other desire in my heart, I speak truly and you are the inner self of all; grant me full bhakti and a mind free of kama and other faults.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Hanuman honours the offered rest and declines it: there is no rest for him until Ram's work is done.

heals.why: a kind offer of ease is thanked and passed

cultivates.why: the task comes before rest
the work is Ram's, not his own

commentary.reading: Mainaka rises from the sea to rest Hanuman; he touches it, bows, and says: without doing Ram's work, where is rest for me. Courtesy and resolve together.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Not for the exhausted: shown to someone burnt out it reads as an order to keep going.

claim: Vibhishan, with no practice and no love to show, takes hope: one meets a saint only by Hari's grace.

depicts.why: a tamasic body, no sadhana, no love in his mind

heals.why: the meeting itself is evidence that grace has reached him
a like-minded friend appears in the enemy's city

cultivates.why: hope born from one good meeting

commentary.reading: Vibhishan to Hanuman: my body is tamasa, I have no sadhana nor love for his feet; yet now I have confidence, Hanuman, for without Hari's kripa saints are not met.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Hanuman says that even on one as lowly as himself Ram showed kindness, and weeps remembering it.

heals.why: he puts himself lower than the one he is consoling

cultivates.why: tears at the memory of kindness received
if it reached him, it can reach you

commentary.reading: Hanuman consoles Vibhishan by his own case: a fickle monkey, low in every way, and yet Raghuvir showed me grace; recalling the Lord's virtues his eyes fill.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'ordinary' softens adham, lowly. Acceptable.

claim: Hanuman asks Sita to hold courage, remember Ram who gives his servants joy, call his power to mind and put away fear.

heals.why: fear is answered by recalling whose strength stands behind her
a messenger is physically there saying hold on

cultivates.why: steadiness asked of the heart
remembering Ram's power

commentary.reading: Hanuman to Sita after giving Ram's message: hold dhira in your heart, mother, remember Ram the giver of joy to servants, bring his prabhuta to mind and give up faint-heartedness.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Monkeys have no great strength or wit of their own, but by the Lord's power a tiny snake can swallow Garuda.

heals.why: smallness is admitted and is no longer the deciding fact
her doubt about small helpers is answered

cultivates.why: strength borrowed from the Lord
the small can take on the vast

commentary.reading: Hanuman to Sita, who doubts the monkeys: we branch-animals have no great bala or buddhi, but by the Lord's pratap a very small snake may eat Garuda.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram protects those who bow to him; if even Ravana goes to him for refuge, he will forget the offence.

heals.why: even the gravest offender is told the door is open

cultivates.why: going for refuge while there is time

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram and owns the wrong

commentary.reading: Hanuman, bound in Ravana's court: Raghunayak is protector of the humble and an ocean of mercy; go to his sharan and the Lord will keep you, forgetting your offence. Ravana refuses.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Sita's life cannot leave her because Ram's name guards her, meditation on him is the door, and her eyes are fixed on her feet.

depicts.why: she is alive only because remembrance bars the way out
her life wants to leave

cultivates.why: name and remembrance as watchman and door

commentary.reading: Asked how Sita preserves her life, Hanuman says: your name is the sentry day and night, dhyana of you the door, her eyes the lock fixed on her feet; by what path can her prana go.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The verse speaks of life wanting to leave the body. Never serve it to a reader with any risk signal.

claim: Ram weeps on hearing of Sita's suffering and asks whether calamity can touch one whose only refuge is him.

heals.why: her pain brings tears to the one she misses

cultivates.why: the Lord himself weeps
the one who relies on him is not abandoned

commentary.reading: Hearing Sita's sorrow the Lord's lotus eyes fill; he asks, can one whose refuge I am in word, body and mind know vipatti even in a dream. Hanuman's reply in the next verse completes it.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: 'Ever truly be lost' is not the verse, which asks whether calamity can come to such a one. As a standalone claim it denies real suffering. Keep it with rcm.5.30.chaupai.2 or use only the first half.

claim: The only real calamity is when remembrance and worship of the Lord stop.

heals.why: outer trouble is ranked below losing remembrance

cultivates.why: remembrance as the one thing to guard
we will defeat the enemy and bring her back

needs: a devotee's frame; said about Sita, whose remembrance never broke

commentary.reading: Hanuman: Lord, vipatti is only when your smaran and bhajan are not; what is a demon to you, we will conquer the foe and bring Janaki.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Offered any reward, Hanuman asks only for unfailing devotion.

heals.why: with everything on offer he wants one thing

cultivates.why: devotion that never leaves, asked as the only gift
nothing else is wanted

commentary.reading: Hanuman to Ram, who has said he cannot repay him: Lord, grant me by your grace the anapayani bhakti that gives great joy. The Lord says evamastu.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram grants that suspicion is sound policy, yet holds to his vow to remove the fear of whoever comes for refuge.

heals.why: the one arriving under suspicion is covered by a vow

cultivates.why: shelter given against cautious advice
a vow kept when prudence argues otherwise

commentary.reading: Sugriva wants Vibhishan bound as a spy; Ram: friend, you have judged niti well, but my pana is to remove the fear of the sharanagat.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: One truly wicked at heart never takes to worship, so whoever comes before Ram is not wicked at heart.

heals.why: the turning toward him is itself evidence of the heart
having come at all counts for him

cultivates.why: trust in what the turning shows

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Ram: it is the sinner's nature never to like my bhajan; if he were wicked of heart, would he come before me.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Vibhishan, having heard of Ram's fame, comes crying to be saved by the one whose refuge brings joy.

depicts.why: the cry of 'save me' from one who has left everything
he arrives with nothing but what he has heard

cultivates.why: he asks for shelter outright

commentary.reading: Vibhishan before Ram: hearing your fair fame I have come, Lord who breaks the fear of rebirth; save me, save me, remover of distress, Raghuvir, giver of joy to the surrendered.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram acknowledges that Vibhishan lived day and night among the wicked and still kept his dharma.

heals.why: what it cost to stay good in that house is finally seen by someone
his conduct is known and named as skilled and upright

cultivates.why: his goodness among the cruel is honoured

commentary.reading: Ram to Vibhishan: you dwell day and night in a company of the wicked; friend, how is your dharma kept. I know all your ways, most skilled in right conduct and averse to wrong.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The verse is a question followed by recognition. Closer: 'You lived among the cruel day and night. How did you keep your goodness, friend? I know your ways.'

claim: Ram at once makes saintly even an enemy of all beings who comes to him in fear, giving up pride, delusion and deceit.

heals.why: no past is beyond being remade
coming afraid is acceptable

cultivates.why: refuge taken with pride and guile laid down

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram and gives up deceit

commentary.reading: Ram tells his own nature: if a man hostile to all creation comes frightened to my shelter, leaving mada, moha, kapat and chhal, I make him like a sadhu at once.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: One who gathers every attachment into one cord tied to Ram's feet, even-minded and wanting nothing, lives in Ram's heart.

heals.why: scattered attachments are gathered, not cut
no elation, grief or fear left in the mind

cultivates.why: the mind bound to his feet
seeing alike and wanting nothing

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Ram: he who collects the threads of mamata for mother, father, kin, wealth and home, twists them into a cord and ties his mind to my feet, dwells in my heart as wealth in a miser's.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Vibhishan admits he came with a desire in his heart, and that love for Ram's feet has carried it away.

depicts.why: he owns that his first motive was mixed

heals.why: a mixed motive did not disqualify him
the wanting dissolved once he arrived

cultivates.why: love for the Lord's feet as the river

commentary.reading: Vibhishan: Lord, knower of hearts, there was at first some vasana in my heart; it has flowed away in the river of love for your feet. Ram crowns him all the same.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Angad enters the enemy's court remembering Ram's feet, with a lion's bearing, steady and fearless.

heals.why: he walks alone into a hostile room

cultivates.why: a lion's gait among enemies
he looks around the court without shrinking
he goes in remembering Ram's feet

commentary.reading: Angad goes into Ravana's sabha remembering Ram's lotus feet, glancing here and there with a lion's stance, dhira, vira and a mass of strength.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Angad sees that the Lord's work accomplishes itself and that being sent is only an honour given to him.

heals.why: the outcome does not rest on him
the mission is an honour, not his achievement

cultivates.why: gladness at being trusted
he goes thrilled, not burdened

commentary.reading: Angad reflects: all the Lord's works are svayamsiddha, he has only given me honour; thinking so the prince's body thrills and his heart rejoices.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The one whom sages cannot reach in meditation and the Vedas call 'not this' plays and jokes with monkeys.

cultivates.why: the unreachable one at play with simple creatures
love brings near what meditation cannot

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: he whom munis do not attain in dhyana and the Veda describes as neti neti, that ocean of grace makes many jests with the monkeys.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Yoga, chanting, charity, austerity, sacrifice and vows do not win Ram's grace as pure love does.

heals.why: one without attainments is not at a disadvantage
effortful practices are ranked below love

cultivates.why: love alone as the means

commentary.reading: Shiva to Uma: yoga, japa, dana, tapa, the many yajnas, vratas and niyamas do not draw Ram's kripa as nishkeval prema does.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: After fourteen years Bharat asks only whether Ram ever remembers him, as one remembers a servant.

depicts.why: fourteen years come down to one question
he hopes to be remembered only as a servant
he is unsure he is thought of at all

commentary.reading: Bharat to Hanuman: tell me, does the gracious master ever remember me as his servant. Hanuman's answer is that Bharat is dear to Ram as life.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The human body is a boat across the sea of becoming, with Ram's grace as the wind and a true teacher at the helm.

heals.why: this life is called a rare and well-equipped chance
the means are in hand and should not be wasted

cultivates.why: a human birth as a gift given without cause
grace as a favouring wind

commentary.reading: Ram to the citizens: the jiva wanders driven by maya; God, the causeless friend, sometimes gives a human body, a boat for bhavasagar with my grace as fair wind and the sadguru as helmsman.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: One who is called Ram's servant and still rests his hopes on men does not really trust.

heals.why: hope hung on people is named as the leak in trust

cultivates.why: final reliance placed in the Lord alone

needs: a committed devotee; this is a challenge, not a comfort

commentary.reading: Ram to the citizens: if one called my servant hopes in men, tell me, what faith is that. By this conduct I am won.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Without devotion even Brahma is dear to Ram only as any creature; with devotion the lowliest being is dear as life.

heals.why: station counts for nothing in being loved
those ranked low by the world are ranked first here

cultivates.why: worth that no status can grant or remove
devotion as the only measure

commentary.reading: Ram to Kakbhushundi: be he Brahma, one without bhakti is dear to me like all beings; a creature with bhakti, though very low, is dear to me as life. This is my word.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: A father loves all his sons alike, yet the one wholly devoted to him is dear as life though unskilled in everything.

heals.why: being skilled at nothing does not make one less loved
the gifted siblings are not the dearest

cultivates.why: single-minded devotion is what the father treasures

commentary.reading: Ram's parable completed: the son devoted to the father in word, mind and deed, who knows no other dharma, is dear as life though ignorant in every way; so with all beings.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Man, woman, neither, or any being at all: whoever worships Ram wholeheartedly without deceit is supremely dear to him.

heals.why: no category of person is outside his love
what others exclude you for is named and set aside

cultivates.why: one's standing with God does not depend on gender or birth
wholehearted, guileless worship

commentary.reading: Ram: purusha, napunsaka or nari, any moving or unmoving being who worships me with all his being, leaving guile, is most dear to me.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The child Ram cries, and his mother runs to him, holds him to her heart and feeds him.

cultivates.why: the ordinary tenderness of holding a crying child
she runs at the sound

commentary.reading: Kakbhushundi: seeing the child cry, the mother rose in haste and ran, spoke softly and clasped him to her breast, kept him in her lap and gave him milk, singing Raghupati's deeds.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: 'The Lord of all cried for his mother' comes from the setting, not the verse. Fine in a story, but it is added.

claim: Devotion to Ram is a wish-granting jewel that lights the heart day and night without lamp, ghee or wick.

heals.why: the poverty of delusion does not come near
the wind of greed cannot put it out

cultivates.why: devotion as a self-luminous gem
a light that needs no tending

commentary.reading: Kakbhushundi contrasts the lamp of jnana, hard to light and easily blown out, with the chintamani of Ram bhakti, which shines of itself.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Devotion to Hari, the fruit of all practice, is found by no one without the saints, as rain reaches us through clouds.

heals.why: what is sought comes through people

cultivates.why: the good as carriers of grace
devotion as the fruit of everything

commentary.reading: Kakbhushundi: Ram is the sea and steady saints the clouds, Hari the sandal tree and saints the breeze; the fruit of all is Hari bhakti, and none has got it without a saint.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'grace reaches us' stands in for devotion to Hari, which is what the verse says is received.

claim: There is no gain like the company of saints, and it does not come without Hari's grace.

cultivates.why: a good meeting counted as grace
grace seen in who one has been given

commentary.reading: Shiva to Girija: no gain equals sant samagam, and without Hari's kripa it does not occur; so sing Veda and Purana.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: In this age there is no other means: remember Ram, sing of Ram, and always hear his virtues.

heals.why: every harder practice is set aside
the mind is given one thing to return to

cultivates.why: remembering, singing and hearing

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: The Manas concludes: in Kali there is no second sadhana, not yoga, yajna, japa, tapa, vrata or puja; remember Ram, sing Ram, hear ever the host of Ram's virtues.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: None is as destitute as I and none befriends the destitute like Ram; so, Ram, remove my dread of worldly existence.

depicts.why: he calls himself the poorest of all
the heavy dread of worldly existence

cultivates.why: his poverty and the Lord's kindness are set side by side as the whole prayer

commentary.reading: Tulsidas's closing prayer: there is none so deen as I and none so kind to the deen as you, Raghuvir; considering this, jewel of the Raghus, take away the grievous fear of rebirth.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet asks that Ram be as constantly dear to him as a woman is to the lustful and money to the greedy.

heals.why: the pull of craving is taken as the model for unbroken attention

cultivates.why: wanting God with the constancy of an obsession

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: The final doha: as woman is dear to the kami and wealth to the lobhi, so may Raghunath be ever dear to me. Tulsidas borrows the two strongest cravings to measure the love he asks for.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The first simile treats woman as the object of lust. The current line already uses only the money simile; keep it that way and do not display the first half as a quote.

claim: Remembering Hanuman frees one from trouble and worry, and his kind glance is a mine of every blessing.

heals.why: remembrance loosens worry

cultivates.why: his glance as the source of every good
his form is a store of joy

needs: devotion to Hanuman

commentary.reading: Vinay Patrika hymn to Hanuman: remembered, he frees from sankat and soch, an image that is a treasury of delight; the monkey's gracious look is a mine of all welfare.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Those in great distress speak without thinking and should not be held to it; the poet asks pardon for what he said in pain.

depicts.why: he said things at the end of his endurance
suffering and fear had become heavy

heals.why: harsh words in extremity are the common way of the hurting

cultivates.why: he asks to be forgiven from the other's side

commentary.reading: Tulsidas to Hanuman: the very distressed, the very needy, the very wretched, do not mind them, they speak unthinking; I was at my limit, Lord, and said it; forgive, looking to your own nature.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: In dire straits one speaks bitterly, and a good master understands and still does good to the one who wronged him.

heals.why: bitter words under pressure are understood by a good master

cultivates.why: trust in the other's goodness after one's own lapse

needs: that the one addressed is God or a truly good elder

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: hard pressed, one says bitter things; the good master hears and understands, and by his own goodness does good even to the ill-doer.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram's name is provision for the destitute, friend of the helpless, family of the familyless and parents to the hungry.

heals.why: every lack is answered by what the name is to that person
friend to the one with no helper

cultivates.why: remembering the name with love

needs: that the reader wants a devotional support

commentary.reading: Tulsidas to his mind: remember with love the name of King Ram, provision of the unprovided, friend of the helpless, fortune of the luckless, lineage of the low-born, limbs of the lame, eyes of the blind, mother and father of the hungry.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Note: 'kul akulin ko' means lineage for one without lineage. It lifts those ranked low by birth and is safe to use.

claim: When the poet said he had no one and clasped Ram's feet, Ram patted his back and made him his own.

depicts.why: 'I have no one anywhere'

heals.why: he is taken by the arm and claimed
his offer to be a servant is accepted warmly

cultivates.why: he holds the feet and offers himself

commentary.reading: Tulsidas recalls his acceptance: as soon as asked I said I will be your slave, I have no one anywhere, and I hold your feet; he stroked my back like a guru, took my arm and owned me.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Hari gave the rare human body out of grace, and only he who tied the soul with delusion's rope can untie it.

heals.why: the knot is not his alone to undo
being bound is not counted as his failure

cultivates.why: he begins by thanking God for a human life
release asked from the one who bound

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Hari, you showed great favour, giving me this body, abode of sadhana, rare even for gods; the rope of moha that binds this jiva only he who bound can loose.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet prays that Ram remove every other reliance and never withdraw his care wherever karma drags him.

depicts.why: his own crooked karma may drag him anywhere
he cannot stop himself going wrong

cultivates.why: every other hope and trust given up
watched over as the tortoise watches her eggs

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: this is my petition, Raghuvir: take away other hope, trust and reliance and the jiva's dullness; wherever crooked karma forcibly carries me, do not for an instant leave off your affection, like the tortoise with her eggs.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet's heart is Ram's house and many thieves have settled in it; his worry is that Ram's name will suffer.

depicts.why: greed, anger and pride have moved in and he cannot evict them
a boundless worry over what this says of his Lord

cultivates.why: the house is handed back to its owner

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: my heart is your dwelling, Lord, and many thieves have come to live there, robbing your abode; my endless care is only that no ill fame come to you.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'Come and see to your own home' is implied by the prayer, not stated in the quoted lines.

claim: The poet longs day and night for Ram's hand on his head, the hand that makes the distressed fearless.

depicts.why: day and night he wants that hand's shade
he is among the distressed who call out

cultivates.why: he waits for the touch that gives fearlessness

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: when, Raghunayak, will you lay on my head that lotus hand which made the afflicted fearless when they once called your name; night and day Tulsidas desires its cool shade.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet both worries for himself and does not: Ram has many like him, and he has only Ram.

depicts.why: he worries and does not, in the same breath
one among countless, with only one to turn to

heals.why: the bond with the mighty one is the reason not to worry

cultivates.why: 'I have only you'

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Ramabhadra, I have care for myself and have not; all jivas in the world are vessels of affliction; you have very many like me, I have only you.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram's greatness is that in his court the wealthy are passed over and the poor are honoured.

heals.why: the poor are the honoured guests here
the world's ranking by wealth is reversed

cultivates.why: dignity that does not depend on means
this has always been the custom of his court

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Raghuvar, this is your glory: slighting the wealthy you honour the poor and show them greater grace; in this darbar the deen are respected, the custom from of old.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Devotion to Ram is easy to speak of and hard to practise; only one in whom it has taken hold knows it.

heals.why: finding the practice hard is what Tulsidas himself reports

cultivates.why: honesty about difficulty from a master of the path

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: the bhakti of Raghupati is hard in the doing; easy to tell, its practice is boundless, and he alone knows it to whom it has come.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet longs to live as a saint: content, wanting nothing, devoted to others' good, unburned by harsh words, even in joy and sorrow.

heals.why: hearing harsh words and not burning
wanting nothing from anyone

cultivates.why: content with what comes
bearing joy and sorrow with an even mind
an aspiration held as a question to oneself

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: will I ever live in this way, by Raghunath's grace taking on a saint's nature: content with what is gained, intent on others' good, unburnt by harsh speech, prideless, cool, bearing dukh and sukh alike.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Even if Ram abandons him, the poet will not abandon Ram, who is father and mother to a bad son.

depicts.why: he pictures being left
a poor beggar and a bad son

cultivates.why: a vow that does not depend on the answer
he will not leave

needs: that this is said to God; never a model for holding on to a person who has left or harmed you

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: if you forsake me, Ram, I will not forsake you; leaving your feet whom shall I love; I am a bad beggar and you the good giver, I a bad son and you my well-wishing father and mother.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Terrified of his own karma as Sugriva was of Bali, the poet asks to live in the shelter of Ram's arm.

depicts.why: his own past pursues him like a stronger brother
no other place and no other prop

cultivates.why: he asks only to be looked at and sheltered

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: somehow, ocean of grace, look toward me, I have no other place; karma is the monkey-king Bali and I am terrified; lord of the lordless, I want to dwell under your arm.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet hands the finding of a way to Ram, by whose glance a losing throw wins and the unseen is seen.

depicts.why: he has run out of his own plans

heals.why: the working out is handed over
what he cannot see or grasp can be shown to him

cultivates.why: 'you find the way'

needs: surrender after effort, not in place of it

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: father, I am your sacrifice, you devise the means; at your mere glance a lost throw falls well; by your showing the unseeable is seen, by your teaching the unknowable known.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The line reads as a promise of a win. The verse is a handing over: 'Father, you find the way. Only your glance can turn this losing throw.'

claim: On a hard road with no provisions and the way forgotten, keep walking saying Ram's name.

depicts.why: he has forgotten the name of his own village
a hard road and nothing to eat on it

cultivates.why: keep walking
the name as the one thing to carry

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Tulsidas's marching song: go on saying Ram, brother, else you fall into the forced labour of rebirth; the path is impassable, no provision with me, the village's name forgotten; Ram, be favourable now.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: However sinful, one who takes shelter of the name is kept by Ram like a coin tied in his cloth, never tested again.

heals.why: once taken in, one is not re-examined
the fear of being found counterfeit is ended

cultivates.why: taking cover behind the name
acceptance that is not on probation

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: however vile a sinner, whoever took the shelter of the name, Ram tied him in his knot like money and never again assayed him true or false.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: A human body is gained to no purpose if one never, in body, word or mind, helps another's work.

heals.why: a use for one's life is named
a life lived only for oneself is called a loss

cultivates.why: helping with someone else's work

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: what gain in having the human body if, by body, speech or mind, even in dream, one is never of use in another's work.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Not a devotional line. Keep it away from exhausted caregivers, for whom it reads as a demand for more.

claim: If there were anyone else to turn to, the poet would not keep coming to Ram in tears.

depicts.why: there is no one else at all
he suspects he is distasteful even to the one he turns to

cultivates.why: he cannot leave these feet

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: were there any other, why would I tell you my sorrows weeping again and again; if you loathe me, hand me to one like yourself; how else can Tulsidas leave your feet.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Let others trust what they will; for the poet Ram's name is the wishing tree and his mother and father.

heals.why: he does not need others to share his trust

cultivates.why: where love and trust are, the work is done
a stubborn child holding to two syllables

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: let him who has another reliance keep it; for me Ram's name is the kalpataru fruiting welfare in Kali; where one's love and trust are, there one's work succeeds; those two letters are my mother and father.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet once wandered hungry, pitied even by sorrow, and by the grace of the name the thorn tree now bears mangoes.

depicts.why: even sorrow felt sorry looking at him

heals.why: a life that began in want changed
the thorn tree bears sweet fruit

cultivates.why: he credits the name for everything he has

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: your name alone, Ram, is my friend; without it I roamed craving for my belly, and grief itself grieved to see me; by the name's grace I, a babul and bahera, now get mango fruit.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'I now bear sweet fruit' and 'now get mangoes' differ slightly; the verse says he, a thorn tree, now obtains mango fruit.

claim: The poet belongs to Ram alone, has lived on Ram's bread birth after birth, and is at peace on that strength.

heals.why: he belongs to a great house
he is someone's, and has been for lifetimes

cultivates.why: cool always on this strength
he names whose bread he has eaten

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: my tongue would rot if I called myself another's; life of Janaki, birth after birth I have lived on your morsel; Tulsidas is ever cool in this strength, I am of a great abode.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: He alone is virtuous with whom Ram is pleased, and Ram is won by natural love; all else is oil on water.

heals.why: the courtesan, the vulture and the hunter reached him without credentials
no pilgrimage or purity was asked of them

cultivates.why: plain, natural love

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: he is the doer of good, pure and true with whom you, Ram, are pleased; ganika, gidh and vyadh went to Hari's city, when did they perfect themselves at Kashi or Prayag; Ram is won by sahaj sneh.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Everyone is good to their own people, but Ram's feet are good to all, and the poor have no other refuge.

heals.why: one who is nobody's 'own' still has a place
the poor are not turned away here

cultivates.why: the one refuge that does not ask whose you are

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: friend of the poor, if you put the poor away they have no second refuge; all are good to themselves, some to their own; your feet, Ram, are good to all.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The more the poet tries to come near, the farther he falls, yet he is Ram's though full of faults.

depicts.why: effort that seems to move him backwards
full of wrongs and faults

heals.why: belonging does not wait on improvement

cultivates.why: 'still, I am yours'

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: the nearer I wish to come, gracious one, the farther I fall; you, Ram, are of one flavour in all four ages, and I am yours though filled with sin and fault.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet vows to lie at Ram's door and not rise all his life until Ram says: you are mine.

depicts.why: he has not yet heard that he is wanted

cultivates.why: a vow made with an oath
he lies down at the one door

needs: that the door is God's; never a model for waiting on a person who withholds acceptance

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: making a vow, from today I lie obstinately at Ram's door; until you say 'you are mine' I will not rise my life long; I swear by the Lord.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The poet will know Ram has accepted him when his mind loves the Lord as naturally as it once clung to pleasures.

heals.why: a test is given for whether one has been accepted
the same ease that fed craving is asked to turn

cultivates.why: love without deceit
joy and tears at hearing the Lord's virtues

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: I shall know you have made me yours when my mind turns back, when with the nature by which it stuck to sense objects it loves the Lord without guile, rejoicing and weeping at his virtues.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ignored at every door where he begged, the poet was told by saints that Ram casts off no one who takes refuge.

depicts.why: he begged door to door with bared teeth
capable, kind people everywhere, and not one spoke to him

heals.why: someone finally spoke to him
he became happy even without love or trust of his own

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: door to door I told my wretchedness, falling at feet; none of the compassionate spoke to me. Seeing me suffer the saints said do not grieve, Raghuvar has not abandoned even beasts and sinners who went for refuge.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: People call the poet a store of faults, but he has one virtue: a sound trust in Ram.

depicts.why: people call him a heap of faults

heals.why: one thing in him is good, and it is the one that counts
others' verdict is not the last word

cultivates.why: trust as his single qualification

commentary.reading: Dohavali: Tulsi has one guna though people call him a treasury of avagunas, a good reliance on you, Ram, who are fit to be pleased by it.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

claim: Straightness of mind, speech and every deed is born of love for Ram.

heals.why: crookedness is replaced at its source

cultivates.why: straight mind, straight words, straight acts
love for Raghuvar as what gives birth to them

commentary.reading: Dohavali: a straight mind, straight speech and all conduct straight; Tulsi, straightness of every kind is the offspring of love for Raghuvar.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

claim: Both clinging to home and abandoning home lose it; one should dwell between house and forest in the city of Ram's love.

heals.why: neither household life nor leaving it is the answer
clinging to home is named as a way of losing it

cultivates.why: detachment without leaving
living in Ram's love wherever one is

commentary.reading: Dohavali: making a house the house is lost, leaving the house the house is lost; Tulsi, midway between home and forest, settle the city of Ram prem.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: 'The city of love' drops Ram. Closer: 'Live in between, in the city of Ram's love.'

claim: The poet, like the rain-bird, has one trust, one strength and one hope: Ram, the dark cloud.

heals.why: hope gathered onto one object
no second reliance to weigh against the first

cultivates.why: single-pointed trust
the chataka's exclusive love

commentary.reading: Dohavali, the chataka dohas: one reliance, one strength, one hope and trust; for the chataka Tulsidas the one friend is Ram, the dark cloud. Ananyata.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: The line drops Ram, the cloud the verse names.

claim: Whether the cloud rains in season or stays indifferent all his life, the rain-bird heart still hopes in Ram.

depicts.why: a whole life in which the cloud may not answer

cultivates.why: hope that does not depend on being answered
loyalty through silence

needs: that the one waited on is God; never a model for staying with a person who ignores you

commentary.reading: Dohavali: whether the cloud rain in time or be cold for a lifetime, Tulsi, this chataka mind still hopes in you.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

claim: Against the treachery of one you trusted enough to sleep with your head in their lap, only the Lord of the world is guardian.

depicts.why: harmed by the very person whose lap was your pillow
no ordinary guard exists against someone that close

heals.why: betrayal by the closest is named as beyond one's power to prevent

cultivates.why: God as guard where trust was broken

commentary.reading: Dohavali: from the ill-dealing of him on whose trust one sleeps with head in his lap, Tulsi, the protector is Jagdish alone.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

claim: A servant who knows his duty is greater than his master: Ram bridged the sea, and Hanuman leapt it.

cultivates.why: service done with full knowledge of one's duty
the servant's leap
the one who serves is ranked highest

commentary.reading: Dohavali: greater than the master is the servant who knows his own dharma; Ram crossed the ocean by binding it, Hanuman went leaping.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: 'Out of love' is added, and the verse's own point is dropped. Corrected: 'A servant who knows his duty is greater than the master. Ram built a bridge to cross the sea. Hanuman leapt.'

claim: Ram does not take to heart even the unfathomable offences of his own people.

heals.why: even faults without bottom are not held
one remains 'his own' through failure

cultivates.why: trust in a memory that does not keep score

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: though his servant's offences be fathomless, he does not bring them into his heart. Same proposition as Manas 1.27, 'rahati na prabhu chit chuk kiye ki'.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Ram himself shades with his own hand the distressed, the poor and those with no protector.

heals.why: the one with no one is covered by a hand
the poor and distressed are the ones he tends personally

cultivates.why: resting under that shade

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: for the arta, the deen and the anath, Raghunath makes the shade of his own hand.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Ram is the poet's mother, father, teacher, brother, companion, friend, son, master and beloved, and his only trust.

heals.why: every relation he lacks is found in one

cultivates.why: dyed in Ram and drawn to no one else
his whole trust in one place

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: Ram is mother, father, guru, brother, companion, friend, son, master and lover; by Ram's oath, my reliance is on Ram; dyed in Ram, my liking delights in none else.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: For the poet, speaking only for himself, the fruit of living is to have mind, goal, love and strength in Ram.

heals.why: he states what his life is for

cultivates.why: mind, refuge, love and strength in Ram
he does not impose his view on others

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: understanding in Ram, refuge in Ram, love for Ram, strength from Ram; I do not speak for all, in Tulsi's opinion this much is the fruit of life in the world.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Prahlad felt no despair because of Narasimha's strength; if Ram protects, no one can kill, so there is no one to fear.

heals.why: the persecuted child's protector is recalled

cultivates.why: 'whom should I fear'
a known rescue as ground for courage

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: Prahlad had not the least vishada, by the strength of the lion; whom shall Tulsi dread, if Ram will keep, who will kill.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Where countless dangers surround one and no kin is near, Ram, whose servant is Hanuman, protects and is the one helper.

depicts.why: no son, parent, friend or brother nearby
dangers on every side

heals.why: a helper is named for the place where family cannot reach

cultivates.why: one helper in every world

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: where there are a crore of dangers and neither son, mother, father, friend nor kin is near, gracious Ram, who has servants like Hanuman, will keep you; Raghunayak alone is my helper.
