commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: With high tastes, low fortune and no job, land, trade or skill, the poet's game was saved by Ram's name alone.

depicts.why: unfit for the world's ways, no craft, no work
even self-interest was out of reach, let alone higher aims
the belly's hard demand

cultivates.why: the name as the one stake he had

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: mind high, tastes high, luck wholly low; unfit for worldly custom; no service, no mine, no farming, no trade or alms, the dolt knows no craft; Tulsi's wager was kept by Ram's name.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Ram, protector of the distressed, stands present wherever anyone remembers him.

heals.why: presence is as near as remembrance
the protector of the distressed is where one is

cultivates.why: remembering him

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: gracious Ram, guardian of the arta, stands there for whoever remembers him, wherever that is.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Ram comes running when his name is called, as a cow runs with flowing milk at her calf's cry.

heals.why: a cry is enough to bring him
one calls as a calf, with no claim but need

cultivates.why: calling the name
the Lord who responds is greater than the Lord who only dwells within

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: greater than the antaryami is the Ram outside who comes on the taking of his name, running like a new-calved cow at the sound of her calf.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Prahlad does not flee his father's drawn sword and answers that Ram is everywhere, even in the pillar.

heals.why: a child stands before a merciless parent and does not run

cultivates.why: he answers plainly under a raised sword
he will not unsay what he holds true
'everywhere', and 'yes'

needs: a story of faith under persecution; not advice to stay near someone violent

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: sword drawn and no mercy anywhere, he did not flee seeing his father terrible as death. Where is Ram? Everywhere. In the pillar? Yes. At that shout Narasimha awoke.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Whoever goes to Ram for refuge fares well: rich or poor, great or small, wise or foolish, weak or strong, lame or blind.

heals.why: every kind of lack is on the list of the welcome
those refused even water elsewhere are looked after

cultivates.why: walking Ram's royal road

commentary.reading: Gitavali: going to Ram's refuge is good for all, wealthy and poor, great and small, wise and dull, weak and mighty; the lame, the blind, the meritless and unprovided all fared well on Ram's highway.
commentary.source: Gita Press Gitavali tika, plain sense

claim: The Lord already knows his servants' joys and sorrows; a kind look from him is how one knows one is accepted.

depicts.why: he waits for one kind look
he has no wish to recite it all again

heals.why: he does not have to explain his pain to be understood

cultivates.why: he asks only to be looked at with compassion

commentary.reading: Gitavali, Vibhishan: the Lord knows his servants' dukh and sukh, so I have not told mine; look on me with eyes filled with compassion, then I shall know you have made me your own.
commentary.source: Gita Press Gitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Ram never abandons one who comes for refuge lacking everything and with no place anywhere; none is dearer to him than his servant.

heals.why: poor, slow-witted and placeless is exactly whom he keeps
one with no place anywhere is given one

cultivates.why: coming for refuge
he says it with his arm raised before the assembly

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Gitavali, Ram: one deprived in every way, wretched, very dull, with no place anywhere, if he comes for sharan I cherish and do not leave; again and again raising my arm I say, none is dear to me as my servant.
commentary.source: Gita Press Gitavali tika, plain sense

claim: Ram, his strength spent beside his fallen brother, still carries one worry: what will become of the one who took refuge with him.

depicts.why: 'all my strength is spent'
without his brother's arm he has no one to rely on
his chest is full of worry for a dependent

commentary.reading: Gitavali: my whole purushartha is exhausted; without a brother's arm to share calamity, on whom shall I rely; the monkeys will return to the hills and I shall follow my brother, but my breast is full of care for Vibhishan's fate.
commentary.source: Gita Press Gitavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: The speaker contemplates following his brother in death. Keep the current line, which omits that, and do not serve this verse to a reader with any risk signal.

claim: Hanuman is hard as a thunderbolt in body and compassionate in mind, and remembering him takes away the poet's pain.

heals.why: pain is met by remembering a protector

cultivates.why: strength and tenderness in one person
protector of the good and helper of servants

needs: devotion to Hanuman

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: body hard as vajra, a roar in battle, a mind adorned with karuna, righteous and steady; death to the wicked, guardian of the good; remembered, he removes Tulsi's pain.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

claim: For one as poor and weak as the poet, Hanuman is the support he leans on.

depicts.why: poor and thin
he needs something to lean on

cultivates.why: 'my pillow is you alone'

needs: devotion to Hanuman

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: Ram's envoy, wishing tree to Ram's slaves, for one deen and weak like me the bolster is yours alone.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

claim: The poet, once a destitute child begging scraps house to house, was called and raised like a son, and asks not to be forgotten.

depicts.why: a pauper wandering for scraps
he fears being forgotten now

heals.why: someone called him and brought him up

cultivates.why: he remembers who raised him

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: a pauper roaming house to house for morsels, the gracious guardian called and reared me like a child; brave son of Anjani, you took charge; do not forget your own, my trust is in you.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

claim: After every medicine and charm has failed and the pain has grown, the poet tells Hanuman that his delay hurts more than the pain.

depicts.why: every remedy tried and the illness worse
he was told 'you are mine' and help has not come
the delay hurts more than the pain

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: I did many medicines, yantras, mantras and charms, entreated the gods, and it only increases; Tulsi is your slave and you called him yours; your slackness, hero, pains me more than the pain.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

claim: Even while the poet practised bad conduct, Hanuman took him as his own and made him fit for Ram's hand.

depicts.why: he calls his own conduct false through and through

heals.why: he was taken in while still doing wrong
he was made fit, not required to be fit

cultivates.why: he credits the one who cleaned him

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: though I practised base conduct you made me your own; son of Anjani, you purified me and I became fit for Ram's hand.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense

claim: Shiva, the home of compassion who loves the lowly, is asked to show grace.

heals.why: the one prayed to is known for loving the lowly

cultivates.why: an opening prayer for grace

commentary.reading: Tulsidas's invocation: fair as jasmine and moon, Uma's lord, abode of karuna, who has affection for the deen, may the crusher of Kama be gracious.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Shiva and Parvati are teacher, father and mother to the poet, friends of the lowly and his well-wishers without motive.

heals.why: he names divine parents and a teacher as his own

cultivates.why: bowing to them as guru and parents
he counts those who wish him well for no reason

commentary.reading: Tulsidas bows to Mahesh and Bhavani as his guru, father and mother, deenbandhu and daily givers, servants and friends of Sita's lord, his guileless benefactors.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Sati, recalling her own deed, is filled with untold worry, and sees that Shiva in his compassion did not speak her fault aloud.

depicts.why: worry beyond telling as she goes over what she did
she knows it as her own offence

cultivates.why: she notices the mercy of not being shamed aloud

commentary.reading: Sati reflects on her own act with boundless chinta: Shiva, fathomless ocean of grace, did not openly state my aparadha.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The line shows only Shiva's mercy; the verse is first Sati's worry over her own act. Fuller: 'She went over what she had done, sick with worry. And he, an ocean of compassion, never said her mistake aloud.'

claim: Shiva is the all-capable Lord, hard to worship yet quickly pleased by one who undertakes hardship for him.

heals.why: a hard goal is said to yield to effort

cultivates.why: the one sought is ashutosh, quickly pleased
hardship taken on for what one wants

commentary.reading: Narada to Himavan: Shambhu is by nature the able Lord and this marriage is auspicious in every way; Mahesh is hard to propitiate, yet soon pleased when austerity is done.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: A worried parent is told to put away worry and remember God: he who made the child will bring about her good.

heals.why: the child's future is placed in the hands that made her

cultivates.why: trust in the maker's care
remembering God in place of fretting

needs: trust in God; and the action that follows in the story, sending Parvati to do tapas

commentary.reading: Himavan to the distraught Maina: beloved, leave all worry and remember Shri Bhagavan; he who fashioned Parvati will do her good. He then counsels Parvati's tapas.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Parvati is told her longing has borne fruit and she may now give up her unbearable austerities.

heals.why: long hardship is told it may stop

cultivates.why: sustained effort is answered
the goal is granted

commentary.reading: Brahma's voice from the sky after Parvati's long tapas: your wish is fulfilled, daughter of the mountain king; leave all this unbearable hardship, Tripurari will be yours.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: A narrative event, not a promise to the reader. Do not serve it to someone waiting on an outcome as if it foretold theirs.

claim: Shiva, though free of desire, is pained by separation from his devotee.

depicts.why: he wanders, teaching and singing, carrying her absence

heals.why: grief at separation is found even in one beyond desire

commentary.reading: After Sati's death Shiva roams, teaching jnana to sages and telling Ram's virtues; though akama, the wise Lord is grieved by the grief of separation from his bhakta.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Parvati owns that her mind is set past all advice, trusting Narada's word, and wants Shiva alone.

depicts.why: she can state every objection to her own course

cultivates.why: a resolve that hears the advice and stays
she names her 'folly' herself and does not apologise

commentary.reading: Parvati to the Saptarishis: my mind is obstinate and hears no teaching, it would raise a wall on water; holding Narada's word true I would fly without wings; see my aviveka, I want Shiva always as husband.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: One who lives beneath the wishing tree should not suffer want; so Parvati asks Shiva to remove her confusion.

depicts.why: a heavy confusion she cannot clear alone

cultivates.why: she asks her question plainly of the one who knows
she expects that the one beside her can answer

commentary.reading: Parvati to Shiva on Kailash: can one whose house is under the kalpataru bear the pain born of poverty; thinking so, moon-crested one, remove the great delusion of my mind.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'You are my shelter' is implied, not stated.

claim: The formless and the personal God are not different; the unborn, unseen One takes form out of love for devotees.

heals.why: the doubt whether the formless can be a person is answered

cultivates.why: form as an act of love
an honest theological question honoured with an answer

commentary.reading: Shiva to Parvati: between saguna and aguna there is no difference, say munis, Puranas and Vedas; the aguna, formless, unseen, unborn becomes saguna under the sway of the bhakta's love.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Even an involuntary utterance of his name burns the sins of many births, and reverent remembrance makes the world's ocean a hoofprint.

heals.why: wrongs of many lives are burnt by the name
the vast crossing shrinks to a puddle

cultivates.why: remembering with reverence

needs: that the reader wants a devotional practice

commentary.reading: Shiva: men who say his name even helplessly burn the sins amassed in many births; those who remember with reverence cross bhavasagar like a cow's footprint.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: A teacher's words, cool as moonlight, removed the heat of delusion and every doubt.

heals.why: a long-carried doubt is gone after being heard and answered

cultivates.why: she tells her teacher what his words did
coolness after the heat of confusion

commentary.reading: Parvati to Shiva: hearing your speech like moon-rays, the heavy autumn heat of my moha is gone; gracious one, you removed all doubt and I have come to know Ram's true nature.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram's heart stays always with Sita, and in that she is to know the whole of his love.

heals.why: the absent one's heart is said to be with her always
the measure of his love is given in one sentence

commentary.reading: Ram's message concludes: that mind of mine dwells ever with you; know the essence of my love in just this. Hearing it, Vaidehi is lost in love and forgets her body.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Sita asks Ram, who lacks nothing, to remember his vow of kindness to the helpless and remove her heavy trouble.

depicts.why: she calls her trouble heavy and herself helpless
the message is all she can send

cultivates.why: she appeals to his own promise

commentary.reading: Sita's message through Hanuman: give my pranam and say, Lord, you are purnakama in every way; remembering your fame as deendayal, take away my great sankat.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Bharat lies on the ground and will not rise, and Ram lifts him by force and holds him to his heart, weeping.

depicts.why: after fourteen years he cannot raise himself from the ground

heals.why: he is lifted without having to earn it
the one he waited for is in tears too

commentary.reading: Bharat, fallen on the earth, does not rise though raised; the ocean of grace lifts him by force to his breast, his dark body thrilling and his lotus eyes overflowing.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram answers Shabari's self-abasement by saying he recognises only one kinship, that of devotion.

heals.why: birth, sex and station are set aside by Ram himself
the world's ranking of her is overturned

cultivates.why: her standing rests on her love, not her category
devotion as the only tie he counts

commentary.reading: Shabari calls herself lowest among women, who are counted lowest of the low; Ram replies, listen, bhamini, I honour only the relation of bhakti, and then lists what does not count: caste, family, wealth, skill.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The first half-line calls women the lowest of the low. Ram's reply overturns it, but the words must never be shown or quoted alone. Also 'I don't measure people the way the world does' is invented. Corrected: 'I recognise only one kinship: the kinship of devotion.' If the app must display the full couplet, drop this verse.

claim: Ram is tender-hearted and gracious without cause: to a flesh-eating vulture he gave the end yogis beg for.

heals.why: the lowliest creature receives what sages seek
nothing about one's nature bars his grace

cultivates.why: kindness that needs no reason
tenderness toward the least regarded

commentary.reading: Of Jatayu: Raghunath is soft-hearted, most compassionate to the deen and gracious without cause; to a vulture, a low bird eating flesh, he gave the gati yogis ask for.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram sends his companions home, telling them to remember him and fear no one.

heals.why: they leave his presence with an instruction not to be afraid
parting comes with a way to stay connected

cultivates.why: fearing no one
remembering him at home

commentary.reading: After the war Ram tells the monkeys and bears: go now each to his home, remember me and fear no one. They are overcome with love.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: By Ram's own goodness Bharat's faults became like ornaments and his good name spread everywhere.

heals.why: what he was ashamed of was turned to his credit by another's kindness

cultivates.why: he credits the change to Ram's goodness, not his own

commentary.reading: Bharat to Ram: Lord, by your own grace and goodness you did me good; my blemishes became like ornaments and fair fame spread on all four sides.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: The sage tells the grieving Bharat not to worry so, for all sorrow will end on seeing Ram's feet.

heals.why: the dread of the meeting is answered by one who knows Ram
an end to the sorrow is named

cultivates.why: trust in what awaits at the end of the road

commentary.reading: Bharadwaj, pleased with Bharat's words: child, do not grieve so much; all sorrow will vanish on seeing Ram's feet.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: 'The moment you see him again' reads as a promise of reunion. For a bereaved reader that is false comfort. Keep it in the Bharat story.

claim: Accepting Ram's command to return, Bharat asks for some support he can serve to get through the years of separation.

depicts.why: he must go back and live through fourteen years without him
he obeys though his heart wanted otherwise

cultivates.why: he asks for something to hold and serve so that he can last
endurance through daily service

commentary.reading: Bharat: now, gracious one, whatever you order I will do with it on my head; but give me, Lord, an avalamb by serving which I may reach the far shore of the term. Ram gives his padukas.
commentary.source: Gita Press tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Every bond joins the poet to Ram: beggar and giver, servant and master, child and parent; he asks only for shelter.

depicts.why: none so helpless or so afflicted as he

heals.why: there are many ties between them and any one will do
a known sinner facing the remover of sin

cultivates.why: 'somehow let Tulsi find the shelter of your feet'

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: you are compassionate and I wretched, you giver and I beggar, I a famed sinner and you destroyer of sin's heap, you Brahman and I jiva, you master and I slave, father, mother, guru, friend; take whichever tie pleases you.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram cherishes the poor and the poet is his poor one, who asks him to say just once: Tulsidas is mine.

depicts.why: he wants to hear once that he is claimed
he names himself Ram's poor one

cultivates.why: a single sentence asked for

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: you are garib nivaj and I am your garib; gracious one, say once, Tulsidas is mine.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: There is nowhere to go on leaving Ram's feet; no one else purifies the fallen or holds the lowliest so dear.

depicts.why: no other door exists for him
he counts himself among the fallen and lowliest

cultivates.why: he stays at these feet

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: where shall I go leaving your feet; whose name in the world is patit pavan, to whom are the very deen dear.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: What was wasted until now will be wasted no more; by Ram's grace the night is over, and he will not sleep again.

depicts.why: the years till now were lost

heals.why: the loss is admitted in half a line and left behind
he will not lay out the bed again

cultivates.why: 'from now, no more'
waking after a long night

commentary.reading: Tulsidas's vow: till now it was ruined, now I will not ruin it; by Ram's kripa the night of worldliness has ended, and having woken I will not spread the bedding again.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: If Ram's grace is with the devotee, no one's enmity can bend a hair of him, whatever schemes are tried.

heals.why: another's ill will is cut down to size
the schemer is denied the last word

cultivates.why: confidence under hostility
grace as the stronger fact

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: if the grace of gracious Raghupati is there, what can another's enmity accomplish; not a hair of the bhakta is bent though one try a crore of devices.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: There is no one Ram failed to protect for the honour of his name; without any cause he removes the whole burden of fear.

heals.why: fear is removed without one's having to deserve it

cultivates.why: his record of keeping everyone who called
compassion that needs no cause

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: who is there whom Raghuvir did not keep for his name's honour; the compassionate Hari, causelessly, took away the whole press of worldly fear.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: No one in the world is as generous as Ram, who melts for the wretched without any service rendered.

heals.why: nothing has to be offered first
having done no service is no bar

cultivates.why: generosity that asks nothing
wonder at being cared for unearned

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: who in the world is so udar; there is none like Ram, who is moved toward the deen without seva.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram is the well-wisher of the lowly: most tender, a store of compassion, doing good to others without cause.

heals.why: the lowly are the ones he looks out for

cultivates.why: kindness without a reason
tenderness as his nature

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas opens the list of Ahalya, Guha, Jatayu and Shabari: such is Ram, benefactor of the deen, very tender, treasury of karuna, helper of others without cause.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram knows the way of love, which removes the greatness of the great and the smallness of the small.

heals.why: smallness is taken away in his love
so is greatness

cultivates.why: equal standing before the one who loves
love as the leveller

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Ram, you know well the manner of love; the Veda honours your fame as one who removes the bigness of the big and the littleness of the little.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The line makes 'love' the subject; in the verse it is Ram's way of loving. Closer: 'Ram's love takes away the bigness of the big and the smallness of the small.'

claim: Day and night the poor poet watches the road for Ram's grace, not knowing when it will come.

depicts.why: watching the road day and night
he cannot tell when it will be
he waits as one of the poor

cultivates.why: he keeps watching

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Lord, wretched, I watch day and night only the path of your grace; at what time it may be, compassionate one, cannot be known.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: Minor: 'but I wait' is implied by the watching, not stated.

claim: The poet asks Ram to keep him in refuge as he has kept him every day until now.

heals.why: the future is asked for on the strength of the past

cultivates.why: 'you have kept me all these days'
asking to be kept

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Ram, keep me in your sharan as you have kept me all my days; the three worlds know there is no second so kind, no protector of the afflicted but you.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Ram's name is the poet's mother and father, kin, teacher, master and friend, and love for it is his lasting wealth.

heals.why: the orphan has a whole family in the name
a wealth that cannot be taken

cultivates.why: steady love for the name
this is his wealth

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: Ram, your name is my mother and father, my kinsman and loved one, guru and lord, comrade and friend; my vow of love to Ram nam is unmoving wealth.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Whatever he is, the poet is Ram's own and asks not to be cast off: a broken arm is still slung from one's neck.

depicts.why: he calls himself an offender
he fears being discarded as damaged

heals.why: what is broken is still one's own and is cared for
the injured eye is tended, not thrown away

cultivates.why: 'such as I am, I am yours'

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: such as I am, Ram, I am your servant, do not forsake me; though guilty, I am yours; the arm though broken hangs at the neck, the eye though hurt aches as one's own and is cared for.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

line_issue: The line keeps the image and loses the plea. Fuller: 'Even at fault, I am your own. A broken arm is still held close in a sling.'

claim: Apart from Ram the poet has no one to tell and no well-wisher with natural tenderness for the suffering and unprotected.

depicts.why: no one else to tell and no one else who wishes him well

cultivates.why: he turns to the one who is tender by nature

commentary.reading: Tulsidas: leaving you, to whom shall I speak, who else is my friend; deenbandhu, who else has natural affection for servant, friend, the afflicted and the orphan.
commentary.source: Gita Press Vinay Patrika tika (Hanuman Prasad Poddar), plain sense

claim: Such as he is, the poet belongs to Ram alone, and therefore it is well with him in every world and time.

heals.why: 'such as I am' is enough
well in all three times

cultivates.why: belonging to Ram alone
settled welfare

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Dohavali: such as I am, I am yours only, lord of Kosala; so who fares as well as Tulsi in the three worlds and three times.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

claim: Hold Ram in awe and give him your attachment, love and trust; one who is wholly Ram's wins even in losing.

heals.why: the outcome no longer decides whether one has won
attachment is given one object

cultivates.why: belonging without condition
defeat and victory lose their difference

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram; surrender after doing one's part

commentary.reading: Dohavali: fear Ram, and have mamata, priti and pratiti toward Ram; Tulsi, on becoming Ram's without reserve there is victory even in defeat.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: The line drops Ram, to whom one belongs. Closer: 'Belong to Ram without conditions, and even losing is winning.'

claim: Sita and Ram guard their own as parents guard a child who plays with a snake or reaches into fire.

heals.why: one is watched while unaware of the danger

cultivates.why: care that works before one asks

needs: that the reader wants refuge in Ram

commentary.reading: Dohavali: the child plays with a serpent and puts its hand in fire; Tulsi, as father and mother guard the infant, so do Sita and Raghunath. Same picture as Manas 3.39.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: 'More often than you know' is invented. Corrected: 'A child plays with a snake and reaches for the fire. As parents keep that child safe, Sita and Ram keep us.'

claim: It is good to step away and good to shield oneself, and not good to strike a wound; Ram stands guard over every head.

heals.why: striking back is the one option ruled out
stepping away is called good, not cowardly

cultivates.why: no wound returned
a guardian over everyone's head
withdraw or shield

commentary.reading: Dohavali: fleeing is good, taking cover is good, dealing a wound is not good; Tulsi, on the head of all the keeper is Raghurau.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: The line drops the practical half. Fuller: 'Better to step away, better to shield yourself, better not to wound. Over every head there is a guardian.'

claim: The poet who begged scraps from house to house without Ram later had kings honour his feet, with Ram as his helper.

depicts.why: he begged for morsels at every house

heals.why: the same person's condition changed entirely

cultivates.why: he names what made the difference
Ram's help as the turning

commentary.reading: Dohavali: he begged crusts from house to house, and then kings worshipped his feet; Tulsi who was then without Ram now has Ram for helper.
commentary.source: Gita Press Dohavali tika, plain sense

line_issue: 'Where you are now is not where you end' is invented and turns testimony into a promise. Corrected: 'He once begged for scraps door to door. Later kings bowed at his feet. The difference, he says, was Ram.'

claim: Born to beggars and raised wailing from door to door, the poet became a mighty master's servant by the power of Ram's name.

depicts.why: four chickpeas looked like life's four goals
his birth brought his parents grief, not joy

heals.why: one lighter than straw was made weightier than a mountain

cultivates.why: amazement at what the name did

commentary.reading: Kavitavali: born in a begging line, my birth was pain to mother and father; from infancy wretched at every door, knowing four grams as the four fruits; that Tulsi is now the good servant of an able lord. Is your name wise or mad, Ram.
commentary.source: Gita Press Kavitavali tika, plain sense

claim: One in whose heart Hanuman's roar rings gladly will be cared for like a child by gracious sages and siddhas.

heals.why: Hanuman's cry in the heart is a guard

cultivates.why: a roar that gladdens
one is looked after like a child

needs: devotion to Hanuman

commentary.reading: Hanuman Bahuk: gracious munis and siddhas will rear like a child him in whose heart Hanuman's shout exults.
commentary.source: Hanuman Bahuk, traditional sense
